https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39e.text: Image source, Oleksandr Hanzha / Dnipropetrovsk regional administration Image caption, A number of people are reported to be trapped in the rubble of the shopping centre in the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 8 minutes ago At least 14 people have been killed in a Russian double-tap drone strike on a shopping centre in the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, local officials have said. Another 121 people - including 22 children - were injured in the city's biggest mall. More people are also reported to be trapped in the rubble. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the "absolutely cynical and despicable" daytime attack in his home town was carried out in "two waves", with the second strike targeting emergency workers at the scene. Dramatic footage verified by the BBC shows the second drone hitting the already burning shopping centre in the Dnipropetrovsk region. Russia's military has not commented. Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said on Friday evening that there were now 14 confirmed fatalities, amid fears that the death toll would rise further. He said that 121 people were injured, including 29 who were in a serious condition. Earlier in the day, Kryvyi Rih Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the Russian drones were flying at "extremely low altitudes", describing the attackers as "animals". "There are missing people who are not responding to calls," the mayor added. This comes a day after 17 people were killed and more than 40 injured in a major Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv. Blocks of flats and warehouses were struck overnight across the city, local officials said. A children's hospital and school were also damaged. Earlier on Friday, Ukraine's military said it carried out strikes on an oil refinery and a military airfield deep inside Russia. Ukraine has in recent months intensified attacks on Russian energy facilities, as well as on warehouses of the country's largest online retailer Wildberries. Kyiv describes them as legitimate targets because they help finance Russia's war. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and currently Moscow controls about a fifth of Ukrainian territory in the south-east. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: A resident of Garvaghy Road, Portadown: there has been growing nationalist self-confidence about a border poll on a united Ireland. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters View image in fullscreen A resident of Garvaghy Road, Portadown: there has been growing nationalist self-confidence about a border poll on a united Ireland. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters Northern Ireland Analysis Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant Daniel Boffey Chief reporter Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.37 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.39 EDT Share Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three Roman Catholic children – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s County Armagh chaplain said at the time. It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then. Northern Ireland is very different place today. Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday. Faced with thousands of members of the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain. View image in fullscreen A march of members of the Orange Order is blocked by police near Drumcree church, Portadown, Northern Ireland, on Monday. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters Every half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful. The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and history sometimes rhyme , more often we hear echoes of history returning to us. The divisions and tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland, papered over by the 1998 Good Friday agreement – when all sides were exhausted by the hate and misery of the three decades of Troubles – have been all too evident of late. This particular dispute can be reasonably argued either way. The independent Parades Commission has ruled that the march down the Garvaghy Road is permissible. The marchers are simply taking advantage of their rights, it may be said. But is it really necessary to take this road after 28 years of the march being banned? Who is served by the provocation? The detail of the argument is perhaps less important than the fact that it is happening, and what that says about Northern Ireland today, and what it may mean for the future. View image in fullscreen Michelle O’Neill, the Northern Ireland first minister (left), and the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, (centre) in the Garvaghy Road area on Sunday. Photograph: Peter Morrison/PA On the nationalist side, there has been growing and bristling self-confidence about the prospects of a border poll on a united Ireland. This was only inflated by Donald Trump’s recent suggestion that a unified Ireland should happen sooner rather than later. “The days of unionist supremacy and domination are gone,” said the first minister, Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, on Monday after appearing herself in Drumcree. “We will not be going backwards.” The numbers gathering from the nationalist community, some of whom were bussed in from Belfast and Derry, appeared to surprise the Police Service of Northern Ireland. It was a moment of unity within an often fractured nationalist community. Those in attendance included Colin Duffy and his brother Paul, who were both acquitted of terror charges in 2015, along with the SDLP party leader Claire Hanna, a vehement critic of those who reach for violence as an answer. Meanwhile, for the unionists, the changed relationship with the rest of the UK brought about by the Brexit deal and changing demographics has arguably engendered a distinct lack of confidence about the future. View image in fullscreen DUP MLA Jonathan Buckley (left), the party leader, Gavin Robinson, (centre) and DUP MLA Diane Dodds at Parliament Buildings, Stormont, on Monday. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP), the largest unionist party, claimed on Monday that “standards have been shattered” by the presence of the first minister with the protesters in Drumcree. When O’Neill and Mary Lou McDonald, the leader of Sinn Féin in the Republic of Ireland, arrived at the protest, it was to chants of “bring it down” and “fuck Stormont”, in reference to power-sharing arrangements in Northern Ireland, structured to make unionists and nationalists work together. “How we can go forward when there is such a level of disdain for the simple fundamental democratic principles of society?” asked Robinson of the attempt by the first minister to block a lawful march. It is likely that the prospect of elections for the Northern Ireland assembly next year, and the need to rally the faithful to their respective cause, is not helping to calm the rhetoric. In Stormont, the speaker, Edwin Poots, a former leader of the DUP, condemned the first minister for her “gross discourtesy” and “contempt” in not coming to answer an urgent question about the crisis. In this context, there is concern that even if Sinn Féin’s leaders, with the crowds’ chants ringing in their ears, do not walk out of the Northern Ireland executive, that the DUP could well do so. View image in fullscreen Members of the Orange Order near Drumcree church on Monday. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters After a prolonged period in which agreement on a budget for Northern Ireland’s collapsing public services has not been found with Westminster, such further fracturing risks a whole new level of instability. The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, spoke to Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, on Monday. The possibility of mediation was discussed, Mac Cionnaith said. Speaking in the Republic, Micheál Martin, the taoiseach, called for cool heads. “No one wants to go back to the past divisions, to past trauma that we experienced at Garvaghy Road, Drumcree, in the past,” he said. “I would say to Sinn Féin and to everybody else: time to dial back now and time to engage in dialogue, and to work this out in a sensible, community-based way.” Explore more on these topics Northern Ireland Democratic Unionist party (DUP) Sinn Féin Northern Irish politics Armagh news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Drumcree standoff shows Northern Ireland’s troubled past still threatens its peace Tensions rise as Orange Order members vow to continue with march blocked by police Loyalist parade in Northern Ireland given go-ahead as almost 30-year ban overturned Drumcree ruling raises fears of sectarian confrontation in Northern Ireland ‘Nobody’s in charge’: is power sharing still working in Northern Ireland? https://astanatimes.com/2026/09/kazakhst.text: Saturday, 10 October, 2026 Almaty 68 °F / 20 °C Astana 52 °F / 11 °C All Stories Nation Astana Culture Sports People Kazakhstan Regions State of the Nation Election 2022 Election 2023 International Astana International Forum Kazakhstan’s Presidency in SCO 5th World Nomad Games Business Central Asia Opinions All Stories Nation Astana Culture Sports People Kazakhstan Regions State of the Nation Election 2022 Election 2023 International Astana International Forum Kazakhstan’s Presidency in SCO 5th World Nomad Games Business Central Asia Opinions Kazakhstan Warns of Global ‘Trust Deficit’ as Foreign Minister Addresses UN General Assembly By Assel Satubaldina in Editor’s Picks , International on 26 September 2026 ASTANA – Kazakhstan called for renewed diplomacy to end the wars in the region while condemning attacks on infrastructure carrying its crude oil through the Black Sea as Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi addressed the UN General Assembly on Sept. 25, warning of a deepening breakdown in international cooperation. Mukhtar Tileuberdi. Photo credit: Kazakh Foreign Ministry “We remain deeply concerned by the Ukrainian crisis, which continues to take lives, erode global trust and undermine international security. Even the most difficult conflicts must ultimately be resolved through diplomacy and negotiation,” said Tileuberdi, who heads Kazakhstan’s delegation at the UN high-level week this year. “Beyond the tragic loss of life, Kazakhstan strongly condemns the repeated drone attacks against eight Kazakh crude oil export infrastructure, including against commercial vessels in the Black Sea basin. Such incidents endanger civilian navigation, disrupt international trade, and threaten the stability of global energy supplies,” he said. Renewed call for diplomacy on the Middle East Turning to the Middle East, Tileuberdi said political and diplomatic efforts remained the only viable path toward ending hostilities and reaching a sustainable settlement. He warned that continued escalation was affecting not only regional security but also economic stability, transport links and energy security. “A just and lasting peace in the Middle East requires an independent, sovereign, and viable State of Palestine living side by side with Israel in peace and security. We support the New York Declaration as a framework for tangible, time-bound and irreversible steps towards the two-State solution,” said Tileuberdi. “Kazakhstan calls for the full and good-faith implementation of the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict and Security Council resolution 2803. As a member of the Board of Peace, President Tokayev has committed to contribute to the stabilization of Gaza, by supporting civilian reconstruction, ensuring food security, and providing digital government solutions,” he said. He also said Kazakhstan had formally announced its intention to join the Abraham Accords, describing them as an additional platform that could reinforce the UN-led political process toward a two-state solution. Afghanistan needs more than humanitarian assistance According to the Kazakh foreign minister, Afghanistan’s stability was inseparable from Central Asian security and development. He called for gradual international engagement coordinated through the UN rather than humanitarian assistance alone. “Humanitarian assistance remains indispensable, but it cannot by itself break the cycle of poverty, displacement and dependency. Kazakhstan supports pragmatic, coordinated and step-by-step international engagement with Afghanistan, with the UN playing the central role,” he said. Preserve biodiversity, not nuclear weapons Kazakhstan also offered to host renewed high-level talks among nuclear powers, linking the proposal to its experience of relinquishing the arsenal it inherited after independence. Mukhtar Tileuberdi held a meeting with UN Secretary-General António Guterres. Photo credit: Kazakh Foreign Ministry “Our small planet is home to more than twelve thousand nuclear weapons, each one capable of untold damage and sorrow. Every year, we seem to lose more biodiversity yet gain more armaments,” he said, stressing that world military expenditures reached a record $2.9 trillion in 2025. “For Kazakhstan, nuclear disarmament in particular is not an abstract doctrine. It is a responsibility born of national experience,” he added. This year marks three important anniversaries: 35 years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk test site, 30 years since the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) opened for signature and 20 years since the Central Asian nuclear-weapon-free-zone treaty was signed. Expressing concern over the erosion of trust between nations, Tileuberdi pointed to the expiration of New START, a nuclear arms reduction treaty between the United States and Russia, and the failure of the 2026 NPT Review Conference to produce a substantive outcome for a third consecutive cycle. He said nuclear-armed states remained bound by their responsibilities despite the lack of agreement and must continue working toward nuclear disarmament. Erosion of trust The international system is becoming less capable of preventing wars and humanitarian crises as trust between states erodes, said Tileuberdi. “The erosion of trust among nations is rapidly reshaping the international order. Our collective inability to prevent conflicts, our collective indifference toward humanitarian crises, and our collective reluctance to seek common solutions to shared challenges are all becoming normalized,” said the minister. “Trust cannot be restored when international law is applied selectively and commitments remain unfulfilled,” he added. Kazakhstan also backed greater Security Council representation for Asia, Africa, Latin America, developing countries and middle powers, which the minister described as a “moral imperative.” “Equitable geographical representation must apply throughout the United Nations system as a condition of legitimacy and credibility. The selection of the next Secretary-General will be one of the defining moments of this session. Kazakhstan supports a transparent, inclusive and merit-based process conducted in full accordance with the Charter,” he said. The address reflected Kazakhstan’s broader effort to place a larger role for middle powers in international diplomacy. Tileuberdi said Kazakhstan would continue pursuing cooperation rather than confrontation, arguing that rebuilding trust would require states not only to reform international institutions but also to honor the commitments they make through them. On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Tileuberdi also held a series of meetings focused on multilateral cooperation, regional connectivity and economic ties. Tileuberdi participated in an informal meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States. Photo credit: Kazakh Foreign Ministry In talks with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, he reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s support for UN reform and discussed the role of the UN Regional Center for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty, while Guterres described Kazakhstan as a “bridge-builder” in an increasingly multipolar world. Tileuberdi also joined an informal meeting of the Organization of Turkic States foreign ministers and held bilateral talks with counterparts from Cyprus, Georgia and Romania, covering energy, investment, transport and logistics, including the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route and the Middle Corridor. Earlier, Tileuberdi also held talks with his counterparts from Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Slovenia, Ukraine and El Salvador, the ministry’s press service reported. https://www.courant.com/2026/10/26/ct-yo.text: Isabelle Roode started running at 17 for the state House of Representatives in the 40th district that serves New London and Groton. She is now 18. (Courtesy) By Christopher Keating | ckeating@courant.com | Hartford Courant PUBLISHED: October 26, 2026 at 5:00 AM EDT | UPDATED: October 26, 2026 at 9:19 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Having recently turned 18, Isabelle Roode represents a new generation of younger candidates seeking to make a difference. Despite her age, Roode started running at 17 for the state House of Representatives in the 40th district that serves New London and Groton. She said she also was not deterred by the political odds in a traditionally Democratic district where Republicans have won only one House election since prominent Democratic attorney Jay Levin recaptured the seat from an incumbent in 1986. “Never let your age convince you that you can’t make a difference,” Roode wrote on Facebook. “I’m proud to represent a new generation that’s willing to step up, work hard, and serve our community! A lot of problems in healthcare, housing, and affordability are system issues. I’m interested in macro-level solutions that prevent problems instead of just responding to them after the fact. That’s the perspective I’m bringing into this campaign.” To a question posed to her, Roode noted , “One solution I support is expanding attainable housing by reducing unnecessary barriers to construction. Connecticut needs more starter homes, duplexes, and workforce housing that middle-class families can realistically afford.” Ironically, Roode, who is a student and runs a business, and recently noted online that she had just voted for the first time, is running against the youngest sitting member of the House, 26-year-old Dan Gaiewski of Groton, a Democrat who is seeking re-election. He is a newcomer himself to the legislature, having won a special election last year to replace Rep. Christine Conley after she departed to become a state Worker Compensation Commission judge. “I think we are certainly seeing a young movement with the Republican Party,” House GOP leader Vincent Candelora told The Courant in an interview. “A lot of them have become more active at the college level, and we’re seeing that where they want to serve in public office. Traditionally, we used to see that with the Democrat Party, but I think it’s good to equally now see that youth engagement with the Republican Party as well.” Candelora added, “Generally speaking, there’s a common theme. A lot of these kids want to run on government overreach. They’re starting to push back to show there is an American Dream, and they want a less intrusive government that taxes less and spends less. … Where you’re seeing a socialist movement in the Democrat Party, you’re conversely seeing more of a freedom movement in the Republican Party. Those are two competing youth movements that we are seeing in this country.” (Aaron Flaum/Hartford Courant) Republican state Rep. Vincent Candelora of North Branford (File photo) House Speaker Matt Ritter of Hartford, who oversees the 102-member Democratic caucus, said, “To be a candidate that young probably means that there weren’t a lot of people willing to run in your district. “That’s probably true for Democrats who ran at that very young age and likewise for Republicans at a young age. Probably there was an opening because people who had served on a local board just weren’t willing to run” for the state legislature, Ritter said. In the Groton-New London race, Ritter said that Gaiewski has started to make his mark as the youngest Democrat in the House. He has joined forces at times with deputy House Speaker pro tempore Bob Godfrey of Danbury, one of the legislature’s older and wisest members who was first elected in 1988, long before the candidates were born. “People always talk about politics as sort of an old person’s business,” Ritter told The Courant. “It’s great to see young candidates. It’s a fascinating race to have two young kids.” The young candidates, he said, bring new ideas to the table. “The two of them combined are 44, which is my age, so it makes me check the mirror for gray hairs,” Ritter said. “I am a believer that the legislature should be diverse in all respects. That also includes the age of our members and the profession of our members. It goes beyond just race and gender and things like that. Any time you are adding an 18- or 26-year-old to a debate with an 80-year-old person with a ton of experience, it’s interesting to hear those perspectives. That’s what a good legislative body is, it’s diverse.” House Speaker Matt Ritter of Hartford is under consideration to be the interim president of the University of Connecticut if UConn president Radenka Maric accepts a job at another university. Here, Ritter reacts while watching a video honoring retiring state representatives on the final day of the General Assembly session at the state Capitol in Hartford on May 6, 2026. (Aaron Flaum/Hartford Courant) West Hartford to Woodstock In other races, 18-year-old Republican Philip Tummescheit is running for an open seat in the 18th district in West Hartford that is currently held by state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest, who did not seek reelection to the legislature as she was running unsuccessfully in a primary against U.S. Rep. John B. Larson. Tummescheit is battling against Democrat Tiffani McGinnis for a seat that the Democrats have held since the 1970s and has been represented by Joan Kemler, Miles Rapoport, Andrew Fleischmann and Gilchrest. In Coventry, 21-year-old William Gifford i s running for an open seat currently held by longtime state Rep. Tim Ackert, who ran unsuccessfully on a ticket with former New Britain Mayor Erin Stewart, who dropped out of the governor’s race amid controversy. After a public records request by The Hartford Courant, New Britain city records showed that Stewart used the city’s credit card to purchase diapers, cosmetics, a yoga mat, clothing for men, women and children, a lighted vanity mirror, power tools, beach and pool toys, children’s toys, bed linens, table cloths and home decorations. Most of the items were classified as office supplies, and about half had receipts. Gifford is running against Democrat Francis Lombard in the 8th district, which covers the entire towns of Coventry and Columbia, along with parts of Bolton, Lebanon and Tolland. Gifford ran into controversy when Ritter and Gov. Ned Lamont called for him to withdraw from the race after he posted an interview that he conducted with a Christian nationalist that Democrats say promoted hate. As a journalism student at UConn, Gifford interviewed a former pastor at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s church and asked, “As a white Christian man, is it antisemitic to not like someone because they are Jewish, because of their religion, because they are Jewish and what the Jewish religion says against white Christian men?” Republicans defended Gifford, and Candelora said that he had “asked a question that was posed that he doesn’t agree with or subscribe to, and it’s being turned into something it really is just not.” In Ridgefield, third-generation resident Blake Consentino is running on the Republican line in the 111th District after graduating from high school in 2025. In a campaign video, he spoke strongly against the 8-30 (g) state law that Republicans have sharply criticized for allowing developers to avoid some traditional zoning regulations when building affordable housing. He is battling against Democratic state Rep. Aimee Berger-Girvalo, who won an open seat in 2020 in a district previously led by longtime Republican Rep. John Frey. “This election is not about left or right,” Consentino said in a video that mentioned his long-running family ties that date back to his grandparents. “I’m not running as a Republican or a partisan.” In the 52nd district, Woodstock Democrat Vincent Tocci , who graduated college in May, is running against longtime Republican Rep. Kurt Vail, a retired corrections officer in the state prisons. After Tocci served as an intern, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy taped a video for Tocci’s campaign website that endorsed his candidacy. “I just think he’s the right person for the moment,” Murphy says in the video. “I think you should check him out. He’s somebody I think I’m going to work closely with, and you won’t regret it.” In politics, lawmakers say that age is relative. Legislators established a Young Republican Caucus in the legislature, where the cutoff for the caucus is age 41. That includes state Senate GOP leader Stephen Harding of Brookfield at age 39 and Republican gubernatorial nominee Ryan Fazio of Greenwich at 36. The group also includes the co-chairman, Rep. Joe Hoxha of Bristol; and Representatives Joe Polletta of Watertown, Seth Bronko of Naugatuck, Chris Stewart of Putnam, and Joe Canino of Torrington, who pulled off an upset of deputy House Speaker pro tempore Michelle Cook in a recount at the age of 27. While both sides have some young candidates, Democrats believe that the deep unpopularity of Republican President Donald J. Trump will help them increase their margin on November 3 in the state House of Representatives, which is currently veto-proof at 102 to 49. Elderly lawmakers The age ranges of legislators swing back and forth as the years go by at the state Capitol. At one point, the state Senate had three elderly, influential senators with years of wisdom in both politics and the issues facing the Senate, Democrats Edith Prague and Biagio “Billy” Ciotto and Republican George “Doc” Gunther . They came from another generation, and their colleagues turned to them for insights that only come with experience. Marc-Yves Regis I, Hartford Courant Linda Bayusik of Bridgeport, hugs Sen. George L. "Doc" Gunther as his wife Priscilla holds his hand at his retirement dinner at The Aqua Turf Club in Plantsville. Sen. Gunther, a Republican, was finishing his 20th term. Born in 1925 when Calvin Coolidge was president, Prague still had the energy that helped her outlast many of her political rivals. She served for years as part of the elderly troika that included Gunther, who died in 2012 at the age of 92, and Ciotto, who died in 2021 at age 91. Prague’s late husband, Franklin, operated an independent chain of more than 20 shoe stores, and her colleagues conceded that they could have lived comfortably in retirement without the Senate job. But Prague kept returning to the Capitol in an attempt to help the elderly — either as a member of the House, the Senate, or as the state’s commissioner on aging. She said that refusing to quit was a trait of her astrological sign, Sagittarius. “I don’t give up,” Prague once said. “When you believe strongly, you can’t give up.” Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Threads (Opens in new window) Threads Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit Most Popular Most Popular Gampel family says UConn name change to pavilion is ‘disrespectful’ Gampel family says UConn name change to pavilion is 'disrespectful' New CT restaurant is opening.
